title: Word 27 — On the Two Fruits of Love for One's Neighbor
attribution_note: Word 27 of 28 in the collection Short Moral-Instructive Words — see Word 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: Many Christians are deceived about the meaning of this word — “neighbor.” Therefore, let us first consider who our neighbor is, so that from this we may know what love for our neighbor truly is.

sections.heading: All People Are Neighbors — Christians Especially So

pairs.en: We are all neighbors to one another: rulers to their subjects, and subjects to their rulers, are neighbors; shepherds to their people, and people to their shepherds, are neighbors; parents to children, and children to parents, are neighbors; masters to servants and peasants, and servants and peasants to their masters, are neighbors; husbands to wives, and wives to husbands, are neighbors; those who buy and sell with one another are neighbors; employers and hired workers are neighbors to each other; judges and the accused are neighbors to each other. In a word, all people — relatives and strangers, acquaintances and the unknown, countrymen and foreigners — are neighbors to one another. But Christians most of all, who are bound together by one faith, one Baptism, one word of God, one confession and invocation of the one God, one hope of the resurrection of the dead and life everlasting. Christians, I say, are neighbors and brothers to one another above all others. For they pray to the one Heavenly Father, and as brothers among themselves say to Him: *“Our Father, who art in heaven,”* and the rest. So then, here we speak of Christian love, which embraces and holds within its arms not only one's own relatives, brothers, friends, and acquaintances, but all people — and especially those near in the faith and brothers in spirit, that is, fellow Christians.

Two fruits of such love are here set forth: the first is to do evil to no one; the second is to show mercy and compassion to one's neighbor in his need. The first mercy and fruit of love, then, is to wrong no one and to do evil to no one.

sections.heading: The First Fruit: Doing No Evil — Toward Parents, Rulers, and Pastors

pairs.en: It is evil not to obey one's pastors and teachers. He who loves does not do this evil, but obeys and submits to them.

sections.heading: Doing No Evil — In Body, in Honor, in Dealings

pairs.en: It is evil to deal with one's neighbor by cunning and flattery. He who loves his neighbor does not do this evil.

sections.heading: Doing No Evil — Within Every Station of Life

pairs.en: It is evil, and an injury to a buyer, when a seller deceives him in his goods. He who loves his neighbor does not commit this evil. Thus *“love does no wrong to its neighbor.”* This is the first fruit of love: to wish no evil to one's neighbor, and to do him none.

sections.heading: The Second Fruit: Mercy in Time of Need

pairs.en: The second fruit of love is to pity one's neighbor in his misfortune and to help him in his distress. He who truly loves his neighbor, seeing him in poverty, cannot help but feel for him, cannot help but be moved to compassion over him, and cannot help but stretch out a hand to help him, for *“love is merciful.”* He sees the hungry, and feeds him; he sees the thirsty, and gives him drink; he sees the naked, and clothes him; he sees the stranger, and takes him into his home; he sees the sick, or one sitting in prison, and visits him [cf. Matthew 25:33–36]. In a word, he helps him in every distress: he suffers with the suffering, grieves with the grieving, comforts the sorrowful, for *“love is merciful.”* The heart of one who loves is stirred over the one he loves when he sees him in misfortune, and so he cannot help but feel for him, and, if he is able, cannot help but come to his aid in that misfortune.

sections.heading: The Pattern of God's Own Mercy

pairs.en: 2) Those who take no care for a neighbor in distress. Such are those rich men who spend their wealth on their own whims and do not help poor people in their distress. They love their own whims, and not their neighbor; and having no love for their neighbor, they have no love for God either. For whoever does not love his neighbor does not love God Himself, as has already been noted in an earlier sermon.

Beloved Christians! Let us strive to hold Christian love in our hearts. It will not let us wish or do any evil to our neighbor. It will persuade us to spend our wealth not on our own whims, but on the wants of our neighbors, and to stretch out a hand of help to them in every distress. Let us love our neighbors sincerely, and let us be true Christians, not false ones. For by this the true Christian is known, as the Lord teaches: *“By this shall all men know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another”* [John 13:35]. Amen.
